opening.headline: Even though the APIs of the three companies that do the same thing have different names and appearances, they have a common structure. This lesson covers finding and reading that structure.
body: Anthropic, OpenAI, and Google all provide APIs for sending questions and receiving answers from models. However, the field names in the request body, the place to put instructions, and the path to retrieve the results are different, so when you try to move one company's code to another company, it becomes difficult to know where to start fixing it.

In this lesson, you will place requests and responses from three companies side by side to find correspondences. And the most important crossroads in design, whether the conversation record is held by the client or the server, is confirmed through examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: Can explain the common structure of Messages, Responses, and Gemini API requests and responses
You can distinguish whether the conversation state is being held by the client or the server.

screens.title: Three APIs that do the same thing but look different
screens.lead: Read it and imagine the calling codes of the three companies laid out side by side. It is good to read while thinking about what is the same and what is different.

visual.alt: A scene where three companies' call code fragments are placed side by side and a question sentence is placed below them.
labels: Even though the names and shapes are different, what is the common structure?

paragraphs: Sending a user's question to a model and receiving an answer is the same for any company. However, the code looks different from company to company. Anthropic uses the Messages API, which receives an array of messages, OpenAI uses Responses, which receives input, and Google creates interactions and reads the results.

The place to write the model name, the place to enter system instructions, and the path to retrieve the result text are all different. If you just list the differences, they look like completely different products, and it becomes difficult to know where to start when trying to transfer code from one company to another.

In that case, instead of memorizing the differences one by one, it is more efficient to first grasp the framework that all APIs share. There is only one question in this class. Even though the names and shapes are different, what is the common structure?

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Just looking at the differences can be confusing, but once you know the common structure, the differences are reduced to a matter of name and location. At the end of class, check to see if this is true.

screens.outro: First, let's think about your experience about where you keep your conversation records.

screens.title: Remember: Who was holding the conversation records?
screens.lead: When you select each question, the instructor's thoughts unfold. You won't have to enter or submit your answer, so think about it in your head first and then press it.

items.prompt: When creating a chatbot or chat app, think about where you store previous conversations.
items.answer: There are several possible answers, including the app's memory, database, and browser state. The important thing is that the model does not remember previous conversations on its own. Someone has to hold onto the conversation transcript and send it along with the next request. The central question of this lesson is who that someone is.

items.prompt: Have you ever asked the same model a second question and it responded as if it didn't know the first question?
items.answer: This happens when previous questions and answers are not included in the second request. It's not that the model forgot, it's that she never received it in the first place. The property of requests being independent of each other is called statelessness, and we explore it in detail in this lesson.

items.prompt: In a web service, think of the difference between how the server remembers the session and how the client sends the necessary information each time.
items.answer: Placing the session on the server makes the request lighter, but leaves the server responsible for storage. The request becomes heavier if the client sends it every time, but you can edit the content at will. The model API's dialog state also has the same options.

screens.outro: Summarizing the experience I came up with in the word request structure, let's first look at the request texts from the three companies side by side.

screens.title: Place request body of three companies side by side
screens.lead: Select each tab to see what the request body looks like for your company. Consider sending the same question, and compare which fields have the same meaning.

tabs.label: Anthropic
tabs.body: Anthropic Messages API sends `model`, `max_tokens`, and `messages`. Each item of `messages` consists of `role` and `content`, and the user's question is included in the item where `role` is the user. Examples in documents always include `max_tokens`. That is, the model, maximum output length, and conversation list are the basic framework of this API.

tabs.label: OpenAI
tabs.body: OpenAI Responses send `model` and `input`. `input` can contain a single string, or a list of items with `role` and `content`. If you're sending it as a list of items, it looks very similar to Anthropic's `messages`. Only the name has changed to `input`.

tabs.label: Google Gemini
tabs.body: The example in the Google Gemini document passes `model` and `input` to `client.interactions.create`, and reads the result as `output_text`. Specifying a model and passing user input is the same as the other two companies. What changes is the name by which the call is made and the path by which the results are read.

tabs.label: common skeleton
tabs.body: Superimposing the three requests leaves us with four: These are model specification, which determines which model to use, user input, which is content sent by the user, output upper limits, which limit the length of the answer, and optional settings such as system instructions or temperature. Although the field names are different, these four roles exist in every company. When moving code, correspond based on this role, not by name.

screens.outro: Now that we see what the request looks like, let's see what comes back in the response.

ext.title: OpenAI: Create a response (Responses API reference)

screens.title: Response structure and usage fields
screens.lead: When you hover over or select an underlined term in the text, the role of that field appears. Check the terms one by one.

data.text: Anthropic's response contains `id`, a role value of "assistant", content block array, and the model used. The content is an array composed of multiple segments resembling a block of type text, so to extract the final text, the array must be read. The response also includes stop_reason. end_turn indicates that the model naturally completed its response, while refusal indicates rejection due to policy. When a refusal occurs, stop_details is also included. Usage is provided via input_tokens and output_tokens within usage. OpenAI provides convenient accessors such as output_text to directly extract the final text, and the Gemini documentation example reads the result as output_text.

terms.tip: The response content is contained in an array of block-like pieces of type text. Since it is not a single piece of text, we read the array and retrieve the text.
This value tells you why the model stopped generating. end_turn means natural end, refusal means rejection according to policy.
Additional information that comes when stop_reason is refusal. Used to check the details of the rejection.
This field contains the usage amount of this call. input_tokens and output_tokens indicate the number of input and output tokens.

This is a convenience accessor that allows you to retrieve the final text directly rather than looking for it directly in the response structure. It appears in the examples in the OpenAI and Gemini documentation.

screens.outro: Now that we can read the response, let's see where the system instructions and conversation state go.

screens.title: System instructions and conversation status: who is holding it?
screens.lead: Switch between the two states and compare how the content of the request changes when the person keeping the conversation history changes.

visual.alt: Two flow diagrams showing what's included in the request depending on where the conversation log is stored.

states.label: stored by the client
states.body: The Messages API is stateless. Since the server doesn't remember previous requests, you have to send the entire conversation history for each request, and you can also create your own assistant turns. OpenAI also allows requests to be independent of each other, so previous messages can be directly concatenated into `input`. This way, you can edit the content at will, such as summarizing or deleting parts of the conversation. Instead, the longer the conversation, the more you have to send each time. System instructions are placed in separate `system` positions for Anthropic and `system_instruction` parameters for Gemini to specify the model's behavior.

states.label: server keeps
states.body: In OpenAI, if you use `previous_response_id`, you can continue the conversation saved by the server just by sending the ID of the previous response. The response object is saved for a certain period of time by default, and is not saved if `store` is set to false. This method has the advantage of requiring less load on the request. However, all input tokens from previous responses included in the chain are also charged as input tokens. Instead, it is a choice to leave the saving of the conversation to the server, and it is difficult to freely edit the content on the client. There is no right answer as to which is better, the choice depends on what control you need.

screens.outro: Let us explain the difference between the two methods in the following explanatory examples. Before that, we'll look at the SDK and file upload API.

screens.title: SDK and file upload API
screens.lead: If you select the right arrow, the flow of uploading a file and reusing it as an identifier will appear step by step. First check what the SDK does and then follow the steps.

steps.title: SDK wraps calls in functions
steps.body: The SDK is a formal library that wraps HTTP request construction, authentication headers, and response interpretation into function calls. Examples in the Gemini documentation show the same call with SDKs for Python, JavaScript, Java, and Go. Even if you send the same request via HTTP without an SDK, the structure is the same.

steps.title: Step 1: Upload your file
steps.body: Large files are not loaded in the body of each request, but are uploaded first through the file upload API. OpenAI's upload reveals the purpose of the file with a purpose value (assistants, batch, fine-tune, etc.).

steps.title: Step 2: Get the identifier
steps.body: After uploading, an identifier (file_id) pointing to the file is returned. Afterwards, you only need to hold on to this identifier without sending the file contents again.

steps.title: Step 3: Reference it in your request
steps.body: You can write the same file repeatedly by referencing the file_id in subsequent requests. Anthropic documentation explains that file_id references are possible on models that support that file type.

screens.outro: Now that we've covered all the request structures and tools, let's move on to an illustrative example.

screens.title: Commentary: Where is the state in a chatbot turn?
screens.lead: The instructor explains one situation in two ways. Select the right arrow to proceed to the next step.

visual.alt: Schematic showing how Method A and Method B requests differ when sending a second query.

steps.title: Situation: Second question
steps.body: The user follows up the first question with a second question: "So what's the price?" Just by looking at this sentence, you can't tell what the price is. For a model to make sense, the first questions and first answers must come from somewhere.

steps.title: Method A: Messages API
steps.body: The app stores the first question and first answer back in `messages`, adds new questions, and sends them all. The server doesn't remember previous requests, so if you don't do this, the model won't know the first question. The app holds conversation records.

steps.title: Method B: previous_response_id
steps.body: The app only sends the IDs of new questions and previous responses. The request is light because the server concatenates the previous contents stored. The server holds conversation records.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: If you want to summarize or erase part of a conversation, A is convenient as the app holds the record. If you want to keep your request light, B is convenient. Either way, the point is that the model doesn't remember itself.

steps.title: Things to check together
steps.body: Since the Messages API is stateless, the `system` instruction must also be sent with each request. Deciding where to place conversation state also determines how to handle system directives and file identifiers.

screens.outro: Now that we've decided on where the state will be, let's see what changes we make when we move the same structure to another company.

screens.title: Commentary: Sequence for transferring one request to another company format
screens.lead: The instructor walks you through the process of moving one Anthropic request to another company format. Select the right arrow to apply the rules one by one.

steps.title: Step 1: Rename the model
steps.body: Let's start with the easiest part. Replace the value `model` with the model name of the company you are moving to. Model names vary from company to company and cannot be left as is.

steps.title: Step 2: Transfer system instructions
steps.body: Move system instructions to the location determined by the company. Anthropic uses a separate `system` digit, and Gemini uses a separate `system_instruction` parameter. Find a place for instructions rather than mixing them into the conversation.

steps.title: Step 3: Format your message
steps.body: Match the `messages` array to the `input` or `interactions` input format for the company you are moving it to. The framework of the item list consisting of `role` and `content` is the same, so you only need to adjust the name and location.

steps.title: Step 4: Change the response path
steps.body: Replace the path to get the text and usage out of the response. Anthropic reads the content block array and usage, OpenAI can use the output_text accessor, and Gemini reads the results with output_text.

steps.title: Step 5: Process large files
steps.body: If the request includes a large file, it is uploaded to each company's upload API and converted into an identifier. Once you've completed this step, the request side, response side, and file processing have all been moved. It's easy to find where you're stuck if you order it in the following order: request, response, and file.

screens.outro: Now, I will conclude by summarizing the contents so far.

screens.title: Location of requests, responses, and states
screens.lead: This screen ties the entire lesson into one picture. Answer the question posed at the beginning.

paragraphs: The first question was, even though the names and shapes are different, what is the common structure? The request consists of a framework of model specification, user input, output upper limit, and selection settings, and the response returns the generated content, termination reason, and usage amount.

The difference is mostly a matter of name and location. All you have to do is check for each company where system instructions are entered and the path to retrieve the results. On the other hand, who holds the conversation state is a matter of design, not name, and must be decided separately.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: The model does not remember previous conversations on its own. Whether the client sends it every time or leaves it to the server to store, someone has to keep track of the conversation.

checks.q: I sent the second question, "So what's the price?" and the model answered as if she didn't know the first question at all. What is the most likely cause in apps that use the Messages API?
options: max_tokens value was too small, previous conversation was truncated
The server did not save the conversation because the system space was empty.
The requests are independent from each other, but the previous questions and answers are not included again in messages.
No input token was recorded in the usage field
checks.explain: The Messages API is stateless, so each request requires sending the entire previous conversation. If you don't include the previous content, the model won't know the first question.

wrong.0: max_tokens is an upper bound on the output length and has nothing to do with remembering previous conversations.
wrong.1: System instructions determine model behavior and do not determine whether the conversation will be saved.
wrong.3: usage only reports usage and is not used to create conversation context.

checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.

checks.q: Match the following terms and descriptions
right: A function to first upload a file, receive an identifier, and refer to that identifier in subsequent requests.
A value that sends only the previous response ID to continue the conversation saved by the server.
Content that specifies model behavior separately from the conversation content
A tool that wraps HTTP request composition, authentication headers, and response interpretation into function calls.
checks.explain: The server conversation connection is the previous_response_id, the call wrapping is the SDK, the reuse of large inputs is the file upload API, and the model behavior specification is the role of the system instruction.
checks.intro: Check for yourself what you just learned. Results are not recorded or graded.

checks.q: Customize the order of operations when moving one request to another company's API format
items: Change the model name to that of the corresponding company.
Move system instructions to the location determined by the company.
Match the message array to the input or interactions input format.
Change the path to retrieve text and usage from the response
Large files are uploaded to each company's upload API and converted into identifiers.
checks.explain: The flow is to change the request side (model, instruction, message) first, then the response path, and finally the large file processing.

glossary.def: Anthropic's interactive request API. Send the role and content in the messages array.
This is the nature of the server not remembering previous requests. The necessary context must be included in each request.
An identifier that points OpenAI to append to the previous response. Used to continue a conversation saved by the server.
These are separate instructions that inform the role or rules of the model. It is placed in a different position from the conversation, and the name of the position is different for each company.
It is a formal library that wraps HTTP request and response processing in language-specific functions.
This is an identifier that points to the uploaded file in subsequent requests.

misconceptions.myth: If the API name is similar, the structure is also the same.
misconceptions.fact: Even though the names are similar, the location of the system instructions and the path to retrieve the text from the response are different. When moving, you should correspond based on role, not name.

misconceptions.myth: If you use previous_response_id, the server automatically remembers everything.
misconceptions.fact: The response to be concatenated must be stored on the server. By default, responses are stored for a certain period of time and are not stored if `store` is set to false. Additionally, previous input tokens on the chain are also charged as input tokens, so reducing the amount sent does not reduce the number of tokens processed.

misconceptions.myth: If you use the SDK, you do not need to know the HTTP request structure.
misconceptions.fact: The SDK wraps the same request in a function. When tracking down errors or moving them to another company, you need to understand the request and response structure underneath.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: The request consists of a common framework such as model, message (role and content), and maximum output length, and the response returns the generated content, termination reason, and usage.
System instructions are placed separately from the conversation, and only the name and location differs from company to company.
The Messages API and Responses requests are stateless by default, meaning that previous conversations must be resent each time.
Previous_response_id is a method of attaching to the response stored by the server, so the amount to be sent is reduced, but storage is left to the server.
The SDK wraps the same call in a language-specific function, and the file upload API allows you to reuse large inputs as file_id.
closing.reflectionLead: The following questions are for self-thinking purposes only and will not be submitted or graded.
closing.reflection: Where are the conversation records accumulated in one turn of the chatbot in my service, and what will change if I change the location?
